EASEMENT AGREEMENT
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

GRANT OF EASEMENT, PURPOSE, AND LOCATION
Pat Morgan ("Grantor"), as owner of the real property located at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, described as Lot 5, Block 2, Tract No. 1234, per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County (the "Servient Property"), grants to Jordan Lee ("Grantee") an easement over, across, or upon the Servient Property for the purpose of vehicular and pedestrian ingress and egress. The specific area, route, or location within the Servient Property that is subject to this easement is described as follows: The westerly 12 feet of the Servient Property, running from the public street to the rear property line.

This easement benefits the real property located at 125 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, described as Lot 6, Block 2, Tract No. 1234, per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County (the "Dominant Property"). This document does not transfer Grantor's title to the Servient Property; Grantor retains ownership of the Servient Property, subject to Grantee's rights under this easement.

SERVITUDES CALIFORNIA'S CIVIL CODE RECOGNIZES AS EASEMENTS
California's Civil Code, in a chapter titled "Servitudes," sets out a specific statutory list of the land burdens that can be created over one parcel of real property for the benefit of another. That list includes, among others, a right-of-way, the right of pasture, the right of fishing or of taking game, the right of taking water, wood, minerals, and other things, the right of transacting business or conducting lawful sports upon land, the right of receiving air, light, or heat from or over land (or of discharging the same), the right of receiving or discharging water, the right of flooding land, the right of having water flow without diminution or disturbance, the right of using a wall as a party wall, the right of receiving more than natural support from adjacent land, the right of having a division fence maintained, and several others including a right of burial and a right of receiving sunlight as separately specified elsewhere in the Code. California's Civil Code states that when this same list of land burdens is "attached to other land as incidents or appurtenances," it is "then called easements." The Code separately states, in the same chapter, that much of that same list of land burdens "may be granted and held, though not attached to land." This easement, stated to be for the purpose of vehicular and pedestrian ingress and egress over the real property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, is created as one of these statutory servitudes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The following land burdens, or servitudes upon land, may be attached to other land as incidents or appurtenances, and are then called easements: 1. The right of pasture; 2. The right of fishing; 3. The right of taking game; 4. The right-of-way; 5. The right of taking water, wood, minerals, and other things; 6. The right of transacting business upon land; 7. The right of conducting lawful sports upon land; 8. The right of receiving air, light, or heat from or over, or discharging the same upon or over land; 9. The right of receiving water from or discharging the same upon land; 10. The right of flooding land; 11. The right of having water flow without diminution or disturbance of any kind; 12. The right of using a wall as a party wall; 13. The right of receiving more than natural support from adjacent land or things affixed thereto; 14. The right of having the whole of a division fence maintained by a coterminous owner; 15. The right of having public conveyances stopped, or of stopping the same on land; 16. The right of a seat in church; 17. The right of burial; 18. The right of receiving sunlight upon or over land as specified in Section 801.5."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 801, California Civil Code, statutory list of servitudes attached to land (easements appurtenant) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=801.)
  "Section Eight Hundred and Two. The following land burdens, or servitudes upon land, may be granted and held, though not attached to land:One—The right to pasture, and of fishing and taking game. Two—The right of a seat in church. Third—The right of burial. Four—The right of taking rents and tolls. Five—The right of way. Six—The right of taking water, wood, minerals, or other things."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 802, California Civil Code, statutory list of servitudes held without attachment to land (easements in gross) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=802.)

This clause does not determine whether this document's particular grant is appurtenant or in gross on its own facts; that depends on whether a Dominant Property is identified and on the document's own terms. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

EXTENT OF AN EASEMENT: TERMS OF THE GRANT
California law states that the extent of a servitude — how broadly or narrowly an easement may be used — is determined by the terms of the grant that created it, or, for an easement that arose some other way, by the nature of the enjoyment by which it was acquired. For an easement created by an express written grant, such as this one, the extent of Jordan Lee's rights over the Servient Property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, for the stated purpose of vehicular and pedestrian ingress and egress, is fixed by the words of this grant itself, including the purpose, location, and any other terms this document states.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The extent of a servitude is determined by the terms of the grant, or the nature of the enjoyment by which it was acquired."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 806, California Civil Code, extent of a servitude (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=806.)

This clause does not determine, on the facts of any particular use, what a particular grant's terms actually permit or forbid. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

INTERPRETING AN EASEMENT GRANT: IN FAVOR OF THE GRANTEE, EXCEPT A RESERVATION
California law states a general rule for interpreting a grant of an interest in real property: a grant is to be interpreted in favor of the grantee. The same statute states an exception: a reservation contained within a grant — language by which the person conveying property keeps some interest for themselves rather than granting it away — is interpreted in favor of the grantor instead, as is any grant made by a public officer or public body, acting as such, to a private party. An easement is itself a grant of an interest in real property — a right to use another's land for a stated purpose. This rule applies to an easement granted outright by Pat Morgan to Jordan Lee, and applies in the opposite direction to the extent this document instead reserves an easement in favor of Pat Morgan rather than granting one to Jordan Lee.

  "A grant is to be interpreted in favor of the grantee, except that a reservation in any grant, and every grant by a public officer or body, as such, to a private party, is to be interpreted in favor of the grantor."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1069, California Civil Code, interpretation of a grant in favor of the grantee, except a reservation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1069.)

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

MAINTENANCE ALLOCATION AND DURATION
This easement is perpetual and shall run with the land. Responsibility for maintaining, repairing, and, if necessary, restoring the easement area described above is allocated as follows: Grantee shall maintain the easement area in good condition at Grantee's sole expense. This document states that allocation as a term of the parties' agreement; it does not by itself obligate Grantor to perform any maintenance, repair, or improvement of the easement area beyond what this allocation states.

RECORDING AN EASEMENT: CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE AND CALIFORNIA'S RACE-NOTICE RULE
Once validly created, an express easement is effective as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee whether or not it is ever recorded; recording is not a condition of the easement's validity between the parties who created it. Recording matters for what it does against later claimants to the Servient Property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814. California law states that every conveyance of real property or an estate for years in it, once acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, serves from the time it is filed with the recorder as constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees. California is a "race-notice" recording state: an earlier conveyance of the same property that is not recorded is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee of that property who takes it in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1213, California Civil Code, recording gives constructive notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1213.)
  "Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action."

AN EASEMENT ATTACHED TO LAND PASSES AUTOMATICALLY ON TRANSFER OF THAT LAND
California law states that a transfer of real property passes all easements attached to it. This means that if the easement this document creates benefits the real property at 125 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 — an easement attached to that property rather than a right personal to Jordan Lee alone — a later transfer of 125 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 by Jordan Lee to a new owner carries the benefit of this easement automatically, without a separate written assignment of the easement itself.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1104, California Civil Code, transfer of real property passes attached easements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1104.)

SIGNATURES, NOTARIAL ACKNOWLEDGMENT, AND RECORDING

I certify under PENALTY OF PERJURY under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing paragraph is true and correct.

SIGNATURES AND DATE: Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee each sign and date this easement agreement below; each name should exactly match the name shown on that party's current identification or title documents, if any.

Signature of Pat Morgan (Grantor): _________________________ Date: _______________

Signature of Jordan Lee (Grantee): _________________________ Date: _______________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF NOTARY: A notary public or other officer completing this certificate verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document to which this certificate is attached, and not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

State of California ) County of _________________________ )

On _________________________ before me, _________________________ (here insert name and title of the officer), personally appeared _________________________, who proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person(s) whose name(s) is/are subscribed to the within instrument and acknowledged to me that they executed the same in their authorized capacity(ies), and that by their signature(s) on the instrument the person(s), or the entity upon behalf of which the person(s) acted, executed the instrument. I certify under PENALTY OF PERJURY under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing paragraph is true and correct.

WITNESS my hand and official seal.

Signature: _________________________ (Seal)

RECORDING: This document affects the title to the Servient Property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814. An instrument creating an easement, like other conveyances of an interest in real property, is customarily recorded with the county recorder in the county where the property is located.
